opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is that language is a tool humans invented for generalization in the first place. Look at the history of AI: we had systems that were superhuman at Go, at Atari games, at specific robotic tasks. But each was trained for one environment, and you couldn't take the Go agent and have it do anything else. It was strong but narrow.

What's different about language? It isn't like Go or chess, where there's one fixed task. It's an open-ended space where you can describe almost anything: a math problem, a piece of code, a feeling, a plan for tomorrow, even a new game you just made up. So if a model learns to operate well in language, it gets a kind of universal interface to many different tasks.

There's also a deeper point that I care about a lot from my work on agents and reasoning. Language isn't only for communicating; it's for *thinking*. When you're in a new situation, you don't have a trained policy for it, but you can reason in words: "What's going on here? What did I try before? What might work?" That ability to think before acting is what lets humans handle things they've never seen. In earlier reinforcement learning, the agent's action space was fixed, like moving left or right. Once you add "thinking" as an action, an action that doesn't change the external world but changes your own internal state, the space becomes infinite. Normally that would make learning harder, but because of pretraining on huge amounts of human language, the model already has strong priors about how to think usefully. That combination is what makes generalization possible.

So in my view, language is powerful not because it's magic, but because it's compressed human experience plus a medium for reasoning. Humans spent thousands of years building it as a tool for abstraction and transfer. Large models are, in a sense, inheriting that tool. That's why I think the path to more general agents goes through language, even when the eventual tasks involve the digital or physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says language is a tool humans invented for generalization and explains that it applies across many different tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that language is the only medium we have that can describe anything, including itself.

If you look at how we used to build agents, say in reinforcement learning, the action space was always something fixed and specific to the environment. In a game you have "move left, move right, jump." In robotics you have joint torques. Each task has its own actions, its own state representation, its own reward, and whatever the agent learns in one place basically doesn't transfer anywhere else. That's the fundamental reason RL stayed narrow for so long. It wasn't that the algorithms were bad, it was that there was no shared substrate across tasks.

Language changes that in two ways. First, as an action space, it's open-ended. A language agent can "do" anything that can be described in words: write an email, call an API, make a plan, ask a clarifying question. You don't have to enumerate actions ahead of time. Second, and this is the part I find more profound, language can be used to reason about language. Thinking, in the sense of ReAct or chain of thought, is just the agent producing an action that doesn't touch the external world at all but changes its own internal context. That's an action with no predefined semantics. The model decides what thinking means in the moment. And that's exactly what you need for generalization, because when you encounter something you've never seen, the only thing that works is to think about it in terms you already understand.

There's also a historical reason it works, which is that humans spent thousands of years compressing their knowledge about the world into text. So when you pretrain a model on language, you aren't just learning a syntax, you're inheriting all the priors about what a reasonable plan looks like, what a sensible next step is, how to recover from a mistake. A reinforcement learning agent starting from scratch has to rediscover all of that through trial and error, for every new environment. A language agent gets it for free and only has to learn the parts that are actually new.

So when I say language is uniquely powerful for generalization, I mean it in a fairly concrete sense. It gives you a universal interface for perception, action, and reasoning, and it comes pre-loaded with human priors. Nothing else we have does both of those things at once.

r001.rationale: The response says language provides a shared substrate that supports generalization across tasks, but it does not identify language as a tool humans invented for that purpose.

astra-6.text:
I think language is powerful because it gives us a shared space for describing very different tasks. You can describe a mathematical problem, a cooking recipe, or a plan for using a computer in language. Those tasks have different inputs and different notions of success, but language lets us express their structure in a common form.

And language is compositional. Once you understand a few concepts, you can combine them to describe a situation you’ve never encountered before. You don’t need a separate demonstration for every possible task. Sometimes an instruction is enough to connect what you already know to something new.

For AI, that creates an interesting bridge between learning and acting. A model can learn from descriptions of the world, then use language to reason about what to do, interpret feedback, and revise its approach. Of course, being able to describe something doesn’t mean you can actually do it—you still need interaction with the environment. But language gives you a very general interface for bringing knowledge into that interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says language helps generalize across different tasks, but does not identify language as a tool humans invented.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is powerful because it lets us express what different tasks have in common. You can learn something in one setting, describe it in words, and then use that description in a setting you’ve never encountered before. You don’t necessarily have to learn everything again from direct experience.

For example, if you learn that a complicated problem can be solved by breaking it into smaller problems, that idea applies to writing a program, planning a trip, or doing research. The environments are different, but language gives you a way to represent the shared structure.

And language is compositional. We can combine familiar concepts to describe a new task, then communicate that task to another person—or to a model. So it’s both a medium for accumulating knowledge and an interface for applying that knowledge. That combination makes it especially useful for generalization.

r001.rationale: The response explains how language supports generalization across tasks, but does not identify language as something humans invented for that purpose.
